scenes.contextualRelevance: Explains fundamental atomic interactions and cosmic phenomena.

narrativeProgression.description: Introduction of the interaction of an electron and a proton.
The electron and proton electromagnetically bond and create a neutral hydrogen atom, called electron capture.
The electron in the hydrogen atom quickly de-excites its ground state by emitting photons in a process called photon decoupling.
The photons from photon decoupling define the cosmic microwave background radiation, which is approximately 2.7 Kelvin.

scenes.title: Electron Capture Scene

scenes.contextualRelevance: Details the process of star formation from nebulae.

narrativeProgression.description: The atoms from hydrogen atom form clouds of interstellar gas and dust called diffuse nebulae.
Diffuse nebulae are stellar nurseries where star formation takes place.
If the gravitational attraction is greater than the force of the gas pressure, the cloud will collapse on itself and form a protostar.
Inside the star, hydrostatic equilibrium is established where the star's internal pressure is balanced by its gravitational pull.

scenes.title: Formation of Stars and Protostars

narrativeProgression.description: Stars evolve through different stages which can be summarized on a Hertzsprung-Russell or HR diagram.
This diagram is a plot of stars by their luminosities, brightness, versus their surface temperature, or spectral class.
Most of the stars lie on the main sequence and produce energy by fusing hydrogen inside their core.

scenes.title: Star Evolution: The HR Diagram

characterInteraction.description: Wanlong Lin uses an orange balloon, that turns red as it inflates, to visually represent the transition of the sun into a red giant. Dàvid Puskàs uses a whiteboard to draw the path of the sun on the HR diagram.

scenes.contextualRelevance: Depicts the lifecycle of a sun-sized star using visual aids.

narrativeProgression.description: The scene explains the sun's journey on the HR diagram.
The mass of the sun is defined as one solar mass.
After being born, a protostar enters the main sequence phase, after billions of years, where hydrogen fuses into helium over 10 billion years.
Once the hydrogen in the core has been exhausted, the sun grows into a red giant and its luminosity significantly increases.
Hydrogen moves to the outer shell, known as the envelope.
At the end of the red giant phase, a helium flash occurs where a part of helium fuses into carbon.
This process continues through the horizontal branch phase.
A helium envelope forms and starts to fuse until it reaches the asymptotic giant branch phase.
The outer shells are pushed away and the planetary nebula is formed.
The final naked core will be a white dwarf with half solar mass.

scenes.title: Evolution of the Sun

videoEditingDetails.description: The screen is split, showing Dàvid Puskàs drawing on the whiteboard on one side, and Wanlong Lin blowing up an orange balloon on the other.

scenes.contextualRelevance: Explains end stages for massive stars and their possible transitions.

narrativeProgression.description: The scene transitions to discussing stars with birth masses less than 8 solar masses.
These smaller stars will never form an iron core and will not become supergiants.
They cannot fuse carbon and heavier elements because they have less gravitational pressure.
The scene transitions to discussing larger stars, those between 8 and 25 solar masses.
Stars this large fuse hydrogen into helium quickly in their cores.
These stars then grow into red supergiants.
They continue to fuse heavier elements until they are left with only an iron core.
Iron in the core cannot go through nuclear fusion so it grows until it reaches a distinct mass called the Chandrasekhar mass of about 1.44 solar masses.
Once the core reaches this mass, it can no longer support itself and undergoes a gravitational collapse, exploding into a supernova.
The collapsed core forms a neutron star, a small, dense star, which cools over time.
Stars larger than 25 solar masses follow a different path after they explode into a supernova.
If the core has a mass greater than the Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff limit of 2.17 solar masses, it evolves into a black hole instead of a neutron star.

scenes.thematicElements: Lifecycle of massive stars and stellar remains.
scenes.title: Life Cycle of Larger Stars
